title: From a Seed
subtitle: How a plant grows, flowers and feeds us
subject: Nature

pages.h: A baby plant in a box
p: A seed looks like a tiny dry stone. But inside is a baby plant, curled up and asleep. Next to it is a packed lunch. The seed will eat that food when it wakes up. A hard coat keeps the baby safe until then.
pages.cap: Inside every seed is a tiny plant, waiting.
pages.fact: Did you know? A seed can wait for years, or even hundreds of years, before it wakes up.

p: A seed needs three things to wake up. Water. Warmth. Air. It does not need light yet. Water soaks through the coat. The seed swells and gets fat. The coat cracks open. The baby plant pushes out. We say the seed has sprouted.
pages.cap: Water is the first thing a seed needs.

p: The root always comes out first. It always grows down. Plant a seed upside down and the root still turns and heads down. Roots drink water from the soil. They also hold the plant tight, so wind cannot pull it out. Some roots go deeper than a house is tall.
pages.cap: The root digs down before the shoot comes up.

pages.q: What comes out of a seed first?
pages.why: The root comes first and grows down to find water.

p: Next, a shoot pokes up. It pushes through the soil toward the light. It is pale at first. Then it reaches sunshine and turns green. Two small leaves open up like hands. Now the packed lunch is gone. The plant must make its own food.
pages.cap: A shoot always bends toward the Sun.

p: A leaf makes food out of thin air. It takes in air through tiny holes. It drinks water from the roots. Sunlight gives it the power. The leaf mixes them into sugar. That sugar feeds the whole plant. Every bite you eat started in a leaf.
pages.cap: Sunlight feeds the grass. The grass feeds the rabbit.
pages.fact: Did you know? Leaves are green because of a colour called chlorophyll that catches sunlight.

pages.h: The tallest tree grew from a seed smaller than a pea
p: A redwood tree in California is more than 115 metres tall. That is as tall as a 30-storey building. It started as a seed about the size of a sesame seed.

Water goes up the stem like juice up a straw. Tiny tubes inside carry it from the roots to every leaf. Then the leaves breathe the water out into the air. One big tree can send hundreds of litres of water into the sky in a single day.
pages.cap: Water travels from the roots to the leaves and out into the air.

p: A flower is bright. It smells sweet. That is on purpose! The colour and smell say, come here, bees. Deep inside the flower is a sweet drink called nectar. Bees love it. While the bee drinks, yellow dust called pollen sticks to its fuzzy body.
pages.cap: A bee lands on a flower to drink nectar. Pollen sticks to its legs.

p: The bee flies to the next flower. Some pollen rubs off. Now that flower can make seeds. This is called pollination. Without the trip, no seeds. One bee can visit thousands of flowers in a day. Butterflies, birds, bats and even the wind carry pollen too.
pages.cap: Pollen rides from flower to flower on a bee.
pages.fact: Did you know? A honeybee may visit 2,000 flowers in one day.

pages.why: The smell and colour invite bees, which carry pollen so the plant can make seeds.

p: After the flower comes the fruit. Fruit grows around the seeds like a soft bag. Apples, cherries and peaches are fruits. So are tomatoes, cucumbers and pumpkins, because they have seeds inside. An animal eats the fruit, walks away, and drops the seeds somewhere new.
pages.cap: If it has seeds inside, it is a fruit, even a cucumber.

p: Seeds cannot walk. So they hitch rides. A dandelion seed has a tiny parachute. The wind carries it away. A maple seed spins like a helicopter. A burr hooks onto a dog's fur. A coconut floats across the sea. The seed lands far from home and grows.
pages.cap: A puff of wind lifts a dandelion seed and carries it far away.

p: You eat seeds every day. Rice is a seed. Bread is made from crushed wheat seeds. Peas, beans and corn are seeds. Peanuts and sunflower seeds are seeds. Even chocolate comes from the seeds of a tree. A bowl of cereal is a bowl of seeds!
pages.cap: Rice, beans, nuts and wheat are all seeds. Weigh a handful.

pages.h: Try it: grow a bean in a jar
p: Watch roots and shoots grow before your eyes.
steps: Wet a paper towel and press it inside a clear jar.
Push a dried bean between the towel and the glass.
Put the jar in a warm, bright spot. Keep the towel damp.
Look every day. In about a week, a root and a shoot appear.
pages.cap: Day by day, the root goes down and the shoot goes up.
pages.safe: Ask a grown-up to help with the glass jar. Do not eat the dried bean, and wash your hands after.

p: The biggest seed in the world is the coco de mer. It grows on a palm tree on islands in the Indian Ocean. One seed can weigh 18 kilograms, as much as you! The smallest seeds come from orchids. They look like dust. A million of them weigh about as much as a paper clip.
pages.cap: One coco de mer seed is bigger than your head. An orchid seed is like dust.

pages.h: The oldest seed to wake up
p: Scientists found a date palm seed in an old ruin in Israel. It was about 2,000 years old. In 2005 they planted it. It grew! The tree is still alive today. They named it Methuselah, after a very old man in an old story.
pages.cap: A seed that waited 2,000 years and then grew into a tree.

p: Bamboo is a giant grass. Some kinds grow almost a metre in one day. You could sit beside it and watch it go. In a few months it can be as tall as a building. Then it stops growing taller and gets stronger. Pandas eat it all day long.
pages.cap: Bamboo can grow about 90 centimetres a day. That is taller every morning.

pages.q: Which of these is a seed?
pages.why: Rice is a seed. A carrot is a root and lettuce is a leaf.

p: A young sunflower turns its face to the Sun all day. In the morning it faces east. By evening it faces west. At night it slowly turns back to wait for sunrise. When the flower is grown, it stops turning and faces east for good.
pages.cap: As the Sun moves across the sky, a young sunflower turns to follow it.

p: In autumn the days get short and cold. The tree cannot make much food. So it stops. The green fades, and red and yellow show through. Then the tree lets its leaves drop. In spring, it grows brand new ones. The tree is not dying. It is resting.
pages.cap: The tree drops its leaves for winter and grows new ones in spring.

p: On a cold island near the top of the world there is a seed bank. It is dug into a frozen mountain. Inside are more than a million packets of seeds from all over Earth. If a plant ever disappears, its seeds are safe there. It is called the Svalbard Global Seed Vault.
pages.cap: Svalbard is so cold that the seeds stay frozen and safe for hundreds of years.

pages.h: Bees help make one in every three bites of your food
p: Apples, berries, pumpkins, almonds and many more need bees to carry pollen. No bees, no fruit. Plant flowers and the bees will come.

pages.h: Try it: look inside a seed
p: Find the baby plant hiding in a bean.
steps: Soak a dried bean in water overnight.
Peel off the thin coat with your fingers.
Gently split the bean into two halves.
Look at the tip. The tiny white curl is the baby plant!
pages.cap: The two halves are the packed lunch. The tiny curl is the baby plant.
pages.safe: Do not eat raw dried beans.
